claims.text: The cast multi-principal element alloy has coarse grains and limited ductility.
Severe plastic deformation followed by low-temperature annealing can produce a dual-phase solid-solution structure with grain sizes below 50 nm.
The proposed processing route can enhance hardness without forming brittle intermetallics.
Low-temperature annealing can stabilize the solid solution against phase separation.
High-pressure torsion or equal-channel angular pressing is a suitable severe-plastic-deformation route for the proposed alloy.
Annealing below the onset of intermetallic precipitation but above the recovery temperature can preserve the desired microstructure.
Grain growth can be arrested by solute drag or second-phase pinning within a narrow annealing-temperature window.
Severe plastic deformation produces a high density of dislocations that contributes to stabilization of the nanocrystalline structure.
Solute segregation at grain boundaries provides pinning points that stabilize the nanocrystalline structure.
The combination of severe-plastic-deformation grain refinement, solute drag, and boundary segregation prevents grain growth during annealing.
Solute drag and boundary segregation suppress the nucleation of brittle intermetallic phases during annealing.
Coexisting FCC and BCC solid-solution phases provide a balance of strength and ductility.
The proposed treatment will produce grain sizes below 50 nm.
The proposed treatment will significantly increase hardness and yield strength.
The treated alloy will retain greater ductility than the cast state.
The treated alloy will contain no brittle intermetallic phases.
The microstructure becomes unstable above the threshold temperature for intermetallic precipitation.
Insufficient deformation strain will fail to generate the dislocation density needed for grain refinement.
